title: Inceptive verbs: serveixo, llegeixo vs dormo, sento
summary: Where the -eix- infix appears, and where it doesn’t.
explanation:
Most Catalan verbs in -ir are inceptive (incoatius): in some forms they add the infix -eix- between the stem and the ending (servir → serveixo). A small group are “pure” verbs with no infix (dormir → dormo). English has nothing like this, so the job is to learn where the infix goes and which verbs never take it.

The infix appears only where the stress would otherwise fall on the stem:

  • present: serveixo, serveixes, serveix, servim, serviu, serveixen
  • present subjunctive: serveixi, serveixis, serveixi, servim, serviu, serveixin
  • imperative: serveix! (but serviu!)

The nosaltres and vosaltres forms are stressed on the ending, so they never take it (llegim, llegiu), and neither do the other tenses: servia, serviré, serviria, he servit, servint. The infix is not a tense marker: serveixo is simply “I serve”.

The pure verbs have to be memorised: dormir, sentir, mentir, obrir, omplir, morir, bullir, fugir, sortir, collir, cosir, tossir. Some of them change the stem vowel: sortir → surto, collir → cullo, cosir → cuso, tossir → tusso. After a consonant cluster the 3rd person singular adds -e: obre, omple.

Valencian uses a different infix (servix, servisc) and Balearic uses -esc- (servesc); this course follows the central standard.

title: Irregular present: faig, dic, vinc, tinc
summary: Fer, dir, venir, tenir, poder, voler, saber, veure: forms to learn by heart.
explanation:
As in English, where the commonest verbs (be, have, do) are the irregular ones, the most frequent Catalan verbs have an irregular present tense. Usually it’s the 1st person singular that “breaks”, while the nosaltres and vosaltres forms stay regular.

  • fer: faig, fas, fa, fem, feu, fan
  • dir: dic, dius, diu, diem, dieu, diuen
  • venir: vinc, vens, ve, venim, veniu, venen
  • tenir: tinc, tens, té, tenim, teniu, tenen
  • poder: puc, pots, pot, podem, podeu, poden
  • voler: vull, vols, vol, volem, voleu, volen
  • saber: sé, saps, sap, sabem, sabeu, saben
  • veure: veig, veus, veu, veiem, veieu, veuen

A typical 1st person ends in -c / -g: likewise beure → bec, creure → crec, viure → visc, conèixer → conec, deure → dec, riure → ric.

The written accent tells apart té (has) and te (you; tea), sé (I know) and se (himself, herself, itself).

Two habits to drop from English: age is expressed with tenir (Tinc vint anys, “I’m twenty”), and with verbs of perception Catalan usually leaves out “can”: Veig el mar (I can see the sea). For the forms of ser, estar and anar, see units 1 and 14.

title: Passat perifràstic: vaig parlar (formation)
summary: Anar + infinitive: all the forms, where the pronouns go, and the literary parlà.
explanation:
The passat perifràstic is the everyday Catalan past tense for completed actions, the equivalent of the English simple past (I spoke, she went). It is formed with an auxiliary plus the infinitive. The auxiliary looks like the present of anar (“to go”), except in the 1st and 2nd persons plural:

  • jo vaig parlar
  • tu vas (vares) parlar
  • ell, ella, vostè va parlar
  • nosaltres vam (vàrem) parlar
  • vosaltres vau (vàreu) parlar
  • ells, elles, vostès van (varen) parlar

The forms in brackets are also standard but longer and less common; in central Catalan speech the short ones dominate. Note: vam, vau, not anem, aneu.

The big trap for English speakers: vaig parlar looks like “I’m going to speak”, but it means “I spoke”. It is a past tense, full stop. Don’t add a: Vaig comprar pa (I bought bread), but Vaig a comprar pa (I’m going [out] to buy bread). And there is no equivalent of English “did” in questions and negatives: Vas venir? (Did you come?) No vaig venir. (I didn’t come.)

Pronouns go before vaig or are attached to the infinitive with a hyphen: Em vaig llevar = Vaig llevar-me; Li vam dir = Vam dir-li. The negative no goes before the whole group: No ho vaig saber.

The simple past (passat simple) is rare in speech but common in books and the press; you only need to recognise it: parlí, parlares, parlà, parlàrem, parlàreu, parlaren. The most frequent irregular forms: fou (= va ser), digué (= va dir), tingué (= va tenir), visqué (= va viure).

examples.ca: Ahir vaig parlar amb la Marta.
examples.en: I spoke to Marta yesterday.

title: Irregular past participles and gerunds
summary: Fet, dit, vist, pres, escrit, and fent, dient, essent.
explanation:
Regular past participles end in -at, -ut, -it (parlat, perdut, dormit). The irregular ones are best learnt in groups:

  • -t / -s: fer → fet, dir → dit, escriure → escrit, treure → tret, dur → dut, veure → vist, prendre → pres (comprendre → comprès)
  • -ert / -ort: obrir → obert, cobrir → cobert, oferir → ofert, morir → mort
  • -gut: creure → cregut, tenir → tingut, venir → vingut, poder → pogut, voler → volgut, beure → begut, conèixer → conegut, viure → viscut, néixer → nascut
  • ser → estat or sigut; estar → estat

Many match common English irregulars: fet (done/made), dit (said), vist (seen), pres (taken), escrit (written). Unlike English participles, they agree when used as adjectives, and the feminine and plural are regular: feta, fets, dita, presa, escrita, oberta, morta, creguda (una porta oberta, “an open door”).

The gerundi is mostly regular (parlant, perdent, dormint), but some verbs, especially those in -ure, have special forms: fer → fent, dir → dient, veure → veient, creure → creient, riure → rient, beure → bevent, escriure → escrivint, viure → vivint, ser → essent or sent.

Don’t use it like English -ing: the Catalan gerund is never used as a noun, and after a preposition Catalan uses the infinitive: Nedar és sa (Swimming is healthy); abans de sortir (before leaving); M’agrada llegir (I like reading).

title: saber or conèixer; saber or poder
summary: Knowing a fact or knowing a person; knowing how or being able.
explanation:
English know has two Catalan equivalents:

  • saber (to know a fact, an answer, a piece of information): Saps on és l’estació? No sé què vol. Often followed by que, on, quan, si.
  • conèixer (to know a person, place or thing, to be familiar with it): Conec la Maria. Coneixes Lleida? Forms: conec, coneixes, coneix, coneixem, coneixeu, coneixen.

A quick test: “know that / where / if…” → saber; “know” + a person or place → conèixer. In the past, vaig conèixer usually means “I met” (for the first time): La vaig conèixer a Girona. Meeting up with someone you already know is trobar-se amb or quedar amb.

English can also splits in two:

  • saber + infinitive (can = know how to, a skill you have learnt): Sé nedar. (I can swim.) Just the infinitive, no com needed.
  • poder + infinitive (can = be able to, be allowed to, have the chance): Avui no puc nedar: fa massa fred.

So “Can you drive?” is Saps conduir? (do you know how?), but “Can you drive me home?” is Em pots portar a casa? (are you able and willing?).

Useful expressions: saber greu, “to be sorry” (Em sap greu: I’m sorry), saber a, “to taste of” (Sap a llimona: it tastes of lemon).

examples.en: Do you know where the station is?
Do you know my brother?

examples.ca: Vaig conèixer la Laia a la universitat.
examples.en: I met Laia at university.

examples.ca: Sé conduir, però avui no puc: he begut vi.
examples.en: I can drive, but not today: I’ve had some wine.

title: The weather: fa calor, plou, neva
summary: Quin temps fa? Fa sol, plou, hi ha boira: weather without “it is”.
explanation:
The question: Quin temps fa? (What’s the weather like?)

English builds weather expressions with “it is” (it’s hot, it’s sunny, it’s raining). Catalan has no “it” and doesn’t use ser here. Most expressions are built with fer (3rd person singular) + a noun:

  • fa bon temps / mal temps (the weather is good / bad)
  • fa calor / fred / fresca (it’s hot / cold / cool)
  • fa sol / vent (it’s sunny / windy)

Rain and snow have their own verbs: plou (ploure): it’s raining, neva (nevar): it’s snowing, calamarseja: it’s hailing. The simple present is the normal way to say what’s happening right now (està plovent is also possible). For other phenomena use hi ha: hi ha boira (it’s foggy), hi ha tempesta (there’s a storm). For the sky, use estar: està ennuvolat (it’s cloudy).

Because calor and fred are nouns, “very hot” is literally “much heat”, so molt behaves as a quantifier. Calor is feminine in Catalan: fa molta calor; but fa molt de fred.

Temperature (in Celsius): Fa vint graus. (It’s twenty degrees.) Estem a dos graus sota zero. (It’s two below zero.)

Don’t mix up the weather and how a person feels. English uses “be” for both (it’s cold / I’m cold), but for people Catalan uses tenir: tinc fred / calor (I’m cold / hot).

examples.ca: Quin temps fa avui? Fa sol i una mica de vent.
examples.en: What’s the weather like today? It’s sunny and a bit windy.
It’s very hot in July.
It’s raining hard: take the umbrella.

examples.ca: Al matí hi ha boira a la carretera.
examples.en: There’s fog on the road in the morning.

title: Duration: fa… que, des de, durant, d’aquí a
summary: Ago, for, since, in: how to say them in Catalan.
explanation:
• fa + period (“ago”). Note the order: fa comes before the period: Vaig arribar fa una setmana. (I arrived a week ago.)
  • fa + period + que + present (an action that is still going on): Fa tres anys que visc aquí. (I’ve lived here for three years.) Same meaning: Visc aquí des de fa tres anys.
  • des de + point in time (“since, from”): des de dilluns, des del 2020.
  • des que + verb (“since” + clause): Des que treballo aquí, dormo poc.
  • durant + period (“for, during”, a period seen as a whole, typically one that is over): Hi vaig viure durant cinc anys. As with English “for”, durant is often simply left out: Hi vaig viure cinc anys.
  • d’aquí a + period (“in” from now, in the future): Torno d’aquí a deu minuts. (I’ll be back in ten minutes.)
  • en + period (“in”, how long something takes): Ho vaig fer en dues hores. (I did it in two hours.)

Watch the tense. Where English uses the present perfect for something still going on (I’ve lived here for three years), Catalan uses the present with fa… que or des de fa. Don’t use durant for a period that is still running.

Watch “in”. English “in” covers two ideas: “in ten minutes” (from now) is d’aquí a deu minuts, while “in two hours” (time taken) is en dues hores. Don’t say torno en deu minuts. In a past story, “an hour later” is una hora després.

Questions: Quant de temps fa que…? (How long have you been…?) Des de quan…? (Since when…?)

title: Indefinites: algun, cap, tot, cada, qualsevol, altre
summary: Some, any, no, all, every, whichever, other.
explanation:
• algun, alguna, alguns, algunes means “some, any” (in questions): Tens algun llibre en català? (Have you got any books in Catalan?) Catalan often uses the singular here. Pronoun: algú (somebody, anybody).
  • cap (invariable) with no means “no, not any” (unit 12): No tinc cap idea (I have no idea). Catalan needs both no and cap: a double negative that English avoids. In questions and conditions cap means “any”: Tens cap pregunta?
  • tot, tota, tots, totes + article means “all, the whole”: tot el dia, tota la nit, tots els dies. Unlike English “all day”, the article is required. Tothom means “everybody” (singular verb, as in English): Tothom ho sap. Tot means “everything”: Ho sé tot.
  • cada (invariable) means “every, each”: cada dia, cada dos dies (every other day). Pronouns: cadascú (everyone, each person), cadascun / cadascuna (each one).
  • qualsevol (pl. qualssevol) means “any (at all), whichever”: en qualsevol moment (at any time). After a noun it means “ordinary”: un dia qualsevol (just an ordinary day).
  • altre, altra, altres means “other”; un altre means “another”: Vols un altre cafè? L’altre dia (the other day).

So English “any” has three translations: algun or cap in questions, cap after no, and qualsevol when it means “no matter which” (Pots venir qualsevol dia).

English “another” is one word, but Catalan always needs the indefinite article: un altre llibre, una altra vegada, never altre llibre on its own.

examples.en: Have you got any questions? No, none.
I’ve been working all day.
The bus comes every twenty minutes.
You can come any day.
Would you like another coffee?

title: Quantity: molt, poc, massa, bastant, gaire, força
summary: A lot, little, too much, quite: which words agree and which don’t.
explanation:
English has different words for countable and uncountable nouns (much / many, little / few). Catalan doesn’t: before a noun, molt and poc simply agree in gender and number: molt temps, molta gent, molts amics, moltes coses; poc soroll, poca paciència, pocs diners, poques ganes.

Before an adjective or adverb, and after a verb, they don’t change; here molt means “very” or “a lot”: molt bo, molt bé, treballa molt, menja poc. A typical mistake is to make “very” agree: una casa molt bonica, not molta bonica.

  • massa (invariable) means “too much, too many, too”: massa gent, massa cotxes, és massa car.
  • bastant / bastants means “quite, quite a lot, enough” (agrees in number only): bastant temps, bastants llibres, és bastant bo.
  • força (invariable) means “quite a lot (of), pretty”: força gent, força cansat.
  • gaire / gaires means “(not) much, (not) many, (not) very”; used only in negatives and questions, much like English much, which also sounds odd in plain statements: No tinc gaire temps. (I don’t have much time.) No hi ha gaires places. (There aren’t many seats.) És gaire lluny? (Is it very far?)

poc vs una mica de works exactly like English “little” vs “a little”: Tinc poc temps (I have little time, not enough); Tinc una mica de temps (I have a little time).

examples.ca: Hi havia molta gent a la platja.
examples.en: There were a lot of people on the beach.

title: Adverbs in -ment
summary: Clar → clarament; two adverbs in a row: clara i ràpidament.
explanation:
Catalan -ment works like English -ly, with one difference: it is added to the feminine form of the adjective:

  • clar → clara → clarament; lent → lentament
  • fàcil → fàcilment; feliç → feliçment (the adjective has one form for both genders)
  • seriós → seriosa → seriosament; tranquil → tranquil·la → tranquil·lament

The adjective keeps its written accent: ràpidament, últimament, còmodament.

When two adverbs come together, -ment can go on the last one only, and the first one stays in the feminine: Ho va explicar clara i ràpidament. English can’t do this (“clear and quickly”), so it looks odd at first. Both full forms are also correct: clarament i ràpidament.

Exceptions: “well” is bé and “badly” is malament; compare English good → well: Ho has fet malament. Catalan often uses de manera + adjective instead, or the adjective itself as an adverb, much like English “fast”: parla clar, camina ràpid.

False friends: actualment means “currently”, not “actually” (= de fet, en realitat); eventualment means “possibly, if need be”, not “eventually” (= finalment, al final); últimament means “lately”, not “ultimately”.

examples.en: Speak clearly, please.
I usually have breakfast at home.
He solved the problem easily.

examples.ca: Ho va explicar clara i ràpidament.
examples.en: He explained it clearly and quickly.
I haven’t been sleeping well lately.

title: però, sinó, sinó que, doncs
summary: Two kinds of “but”, “not… but rather”, “so”, and the si no trap.
explanation:
Where English has one word, but, Catalan has two:

  • però (“but” expressing contrast): És car, però val la pena. (It’s expensive, but it’s worth it.) It can also go inside the sentence, like “however”: La idea, però, no em convenç.
  • sinó (“but rather” after a negative, when you correct a word or phrase): No és italià, sinó francès. (He isn’t Italian but French.) Test: if you can say “not X but (instead) Y”, use sinó.
  • sinó que (the same, but followed by a conjugated verb): No va venir, sinó que va trucar. (He didn’t come; he phoned instead.)
  • no només… sinó (que) també (not only… but also): No només parla àrab, sinó també francès.

Don’t confuse sinó (one word) with si no (“if not”): Si no plou, sortirem. (If it doesn’t rain, we’ll go out.) They sound alike, so the spelling is easy to get wrong.

doncs expresses a consequence (“so, then, in that case”): Tens fred? Doncs tanca la finestra. (Are you cold? Then close the window.) At the start of a reply it is often just “well”: Doncs no ho sé. (Well, I don’t know.) Doncs never gives a reason: “No vinc, doncs estic cansat” is wrong (a calque of Spanish pues); use perquè or ja que.

examples.en: I like it, but it’s too expensive.
I don’t want tea, I want coffee.

title: Cause and consequence: perquè, com que, així que
explanation:
Cause:

  • perquè + indicative means “because”, usually after the main clause: No vinc perquè estic malalt. “Why?” is written as two words: Per què no vens? English has two different words; Catalan only spells them differently.
  • com que means “as, since”; it goes only at the beginning of the sentence: Com que plovia, ens vam quedar a casa. Where English starts with “Because it was raining, …”, Catalan prefers com que.
  • ja que, atès que, vist que mean “since, given that, seeing that” (a cause the listener already knows); they can go anywhere in the sentence.
  • Before a noun: a causa de (because of), per culpa de (something bad), gràcies a (thanks to, something good). Just as English needs “because of”, Catalan can’t use perquè before a noun. Avoid degut a as a preposition (“due to”); say a causa de.

English since can refer to time or to cause; Catalan keeps them apart: time is des que (unit 63), cause is ja que or com que.

Consequence:

  • així que means “so” (conversational): Era tard, així que vam agafar un taxi.
  • per tant, per això, doncs mean “therefore, that’s why, so”: No ha estudiat; per tant, no aprovarà.
  • de manera que + indicative means “so” (with the result that).

Remember: perquè + subjunctive expresses purpose, “so that” (unit 35), not cause.

examples.ca: No he vingut perquè estava malalt.
examples.en: I didn’t come because I was ill.

examples.ca: Com que no tenia diners, no vaig comprar res.

title: Concession: encara que, tot i que, malgrat que
summary: “Although”: indicative; “even if”: subjunctive; tot i + infinitive.
explanation:
English has different words for “although / even though” and “even if”. Catalan uses the same conjunctions (encara que, tot i que, malgrat que) and lets the mood of the verb make the difference:

  • indicative (a real fact, “although”): Encara que plou, sortirem. (Although it’s raining, we’ll go out.)
  • subjunctive (a possibility, or a fact the speaker treats as irrelevant, “even if”): Encara que plogui, sortirem. (Even if it rains, we’ll go out.)
  • imperfect subjunctive (an imaginary situation, like English “even if I were”): Encara que fos ric, no ho compraria. (Even if I were rich, I wouldn’t buy it.)

Careful: encara on its own means “still, yet”; it’s encara que that means “although”. Tot i que is mostly used with the indicative, for real facts.

Shorter constructions:

  • tot i + infinitive (when the subject is the same). English uses “despite” + -ing; Catalan uses the infinitive: Tot i estar cansat, va continuar. (Despite being tired, he carried on.)
  • malgrat / tot i + noun (“despite, in spite of”): malgrat la pluja, tot i el cansament; malgrat tot (in spite of everything).
  • per més que / per molt que + subjunctive (“however much, no matter how much”): Per més que ho intenti, no me’n surto. (However hard I try, I can’t manage it.)

examples.en: Although it’s raining, we’ll go on our hike.
Even if it rains, we’ll go on our hike.

examples.ca: Tot i que estava cansada, va acabar la feina.
examples.en: Although she was tired, she finished the job.

examples.ca: Malgrat la pluja, el concert es va fer.
examples.en: Despite the rain, the concert went ahead.

examples.ca: Tot i tenir febre, va anar a treballar.
examples.en: Despite having a temperature, he went to work.

examples.ca: Per molt que insisteixis, no canviaré d’opinió.
examples.en: No matter how much you insist, I won’t change my mind.

exercises.instruction: Indicative or subjunctive? Put the verb in the correct form.

items.q: Encara que ara (fer) ___ fred, no porto abric.
Tot i que (ser) ___ tard, vam continuar parlant.
No t’ho diré encara que m’ho (tu, demanar) ___ mil vegades.
Malgrat que (tenir) ___ molts diners, viu de manera senzilla.
Encara que (jo, guanyar) ___ la loteria, no deixaria la feina.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite the sentence with tot i + infinitive.

items.q: Tot i que era petit, ho entenia tot.
items.a: Tot i ser petit, ho entenia tot.

items.q: Tot i que va estudiar molt, no va aprovar.
items.a: Tot i estudiar molt, no va aprovar. / Tot i haver estudiat molt, no va aprovar.

items.q: Tot i que viu a prop, sempre arriba tard.
items.a: Tot i viure a prop, sempre arriba tard.

items.q: Tot i que té febre, vol sortir.
items.a: Tot i tenir febre, vol sortir.

items.q: Tot i que coneixia el camí, es va perdre.
items.a: Tot i conèixer el camí, es va perdre.

title: “Become”: fer-se, tornar-se, posar-se, quedar-se
summary: Get nervous, go mad, get rich, go blind, and the literary esdevenir.
explanation:
English expresses change with become, get, go, turn, grow, and with verbs like “blush” or “age”. Catalan has no single verb for this; the choice depends on the kind of change:

  • posar-se + adjective expresses a quick, often temporary change of state or mood (“get, go”): posar-se vermell (go red), posar-se nerviós, trist, malalt (get nervous, sad, ill).
  • tornar-se + adjective expresses a deep, noticeable change of character (“become, turn”): S’ha tornat molt egoista. (He’s become very selfish.) Es va tornar boig. (He went mad.)
  • fer-se + adjective / noun expresses a gradual process, age, effort (“grow, get, become”): fer-se gran (grow up, get old), fer-se ric, fer-se famós, fer-se vegetarià; impersonal: es fa tard (it’s getting late), es fa fosc (it’s getting dark).
  • quedar-se + adjective / sense + noun expresses the result of an event, often sudden or unwanted (“go, end up, be left”): quedar-se cec (go blind), quedar-se sol (end up alone), quedar-se sense feina (lose one’s job), quedar-se parat (be stunned).
  • esdevenir is a neutral “become”, mainly in written style: La ciutat va esdevenir la capital del comtat.

Also: convertir-se en + noun (to turn into); arribar a ser (to end up as, go on to become): Va arribar a ser ministra. (She went on to become a minister.)

Many English “get” + adjective combinations are simply pronominal verbs in Catalan: cansar-se (get tired), enfadar-se (get angry), casar-se (get married), perdre’s (get lost). Never translate this “get” with obtenir or aconseguir.

examples.ca: Quan el va veure, es va posar vermella.
examples.en: When she saw him, she went red.

examples.ca: Des que és famós, s’ha tornat insuportable.
examples.en: Ever since he got famous, he’s become unbearable.

examples.ca: A l’hivern es fa fosc molt d’hora.
examples.en: In winter it gets dark very early.
He was left speechless.

examples.ca: Amb els anys, el poble va esdevenir una ciutat turística.
examples.en: Over the years, the village became a tourist town.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right verb (posar-se, tornar-se, fer-se, quedar-se, esdevenir, convertir-se en) and put it in the correct form.

items.q: Aquell petit taller ___ una gran empresa.
items.a: va esdevenir / es va convertir en

exercises.instruction: Translate into Catalan.

items.a: Els nens es fan grans tan de pressa!
S’ha fet vegetariana. / Es va fer vegetariana.
